items.followUp: Differentiate between active transport and diffusion.

rubric.why: Identifies osmosis as the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that water moves through a selectively permeable membrane, typically from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one.

rubric.why: Identifies diffusion as movement down a concentration gradient.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that particles move from higher to lower concentration.

modelAnswer: Osmosis is the movement of water molecules through a selectively permeable membrane from a region of higher water concentration to a region of lower water concentration.
Diffusion is the net movement of molecules from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a cancerous tumor that spreads and one that remains localized.

rubric.why: Describes the defining invasive and spreading behaviour of malignant tumors.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that malignant tumors are cancerous and invade nearby tissues or spread to other parts of the body.

rubric.why: Distinguishes benign tumors by their noncancerous, localized nature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that benign tumors are noncancerous and remain localized without spreading.

modelAnswer: Malignant tumors are cancerous; they invade surrounding tissues and may spread to other parts of the body.
Benign tumors are noncancerous and remain localized; they do not invade or spread to other parts of the body.

items.followUp: What is crossing over, and when does it occur during meiosis?

rubric.why: Defines disjunction as the normal separation of chromosomes during meiosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that homologous chromosomes separate normally during meiosis.

rubric.why: Defines non-disjunction as a failure of normal chromosome separation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chromosomes fail to separate during meiosis.

modelAnswer: Disjunction is the normal separation of homologous chromosomes during meiosis.
Non-disjunction is the failure of chromosomes to separate properly during meiosis, resulting in cells with an abnormal number of chromosomes.

items.followUp: Write the classification of the human being from kingdom to species.

rubric.why: Gives the pea plant’s kingdom, division and class.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct kingdom, division and class; accept the listed textbook or modern rank names.

rubric.why: Completes the classification through order, family, genus and species.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct order, family, genus and species; accept the listed alternatives for order and family.

modelAnswer: Kingdom: Plantae.
Division: Angiospermae (Magnoliophyta).
Class: Dicotyledonae (Magnoliopsida).
Order: Rosales (Fabales).
Family: Leguminosae (Fabaceae).
Genus: Pisum.
Species: sativum (Pisum sativum).

items.followUp: What is a metabolic pathway? Explain the role of enzymes in it.

rubric.why: Identifies a metabolic pathway as a sequence of reactions in a cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a metabolic pathway as a series or sequence of chemical reactions in a cell.

rubric.why: States that enzymes catalyse the individual steps of the pathway.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that enzymes control or catalyse the reactions, with the product of one step serving as the next step’s substrate.

modelAnswer: A metabolic pathway is a series of chemical reactions occurring in a cell.
Each reaction is catalysed by a specific enzyme, and the product of one reaction becomes the substrate for the next.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a cofactor and a coenzyme.

rubric.why: Gives the defining tight association of a prosthetic group with its enzyme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a prosthetic group is tightly or permanently bound to the enzyme.

rubric.why: Distinguishes coenzymes as organic cofactors that associate temporarily or loosely with enzymes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a coenzyme is an organic, loosely or temporarily bound cofactor.

modelAnswer: A prosthetic group is a non-protein component that is tightly or permanently bound to an enzyme.
A coenzyme is an organic cofactor that binds loosely or temporarily to an enzyme.

items.followUp: Explain how an enzyme catalyses a reaction and is available to act again.

rubric.why: Explains formation of the enzyme-substrate complex at the active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the substrate binds to the enzyme’s active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex.

rubric.why: Explains product release and that the enzyme can be reused.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the substrate is converted to product, which is released while the enzyme remains unchanged.

modelAnswer: The substrate fits into the enzyme’s specific active site and binds to it, forming an enzyme-substrate (ES) complex.
The enzyme converts the substrate into product; the product is released and the unchanged enzyme can be used again.

items.followUp: Name the main secretions of the intestinal glands and give one function of each.

rubric.why: Names the acid and protein-digesting enzyme precursor secreted into the stomach.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming hydrochloric acid and pepsin (or pepsinogen).

rubric.why: Includes mucus, another main component of gastric juice.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming mucus as a component of gastric juice.

modelAnswer: Gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid (HCl), pepsinogen (which forms pepsin), and mucus.
